Find a polynomial certificate for a finite-field inclusion matrix.

All arithmetic is in GF(101); write every field element as its least
nonnegative decimal residue in 0,...,100.

The ground set is X={0,1,...,199}.  Its distinguished
p-element subset B is: [0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 27, 28, 29, 31, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39, 41, 43, 46, 47, 49, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 62, 67, 70, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 81, 82, 85, 86, 88, 89, 92, 94, 96, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 109, 111, 113, 116, 121, 124, 125, 126, 128, 129, 131, 133, 134, 136, 139, 140, 144, 145, 148, 151, 154, 157, 163, 164, 165, 166, 170, 173, 174, 175, 176, 186, 187, 190, 193, 194, 196, 198, 199]

For every (99)-element subset A of X, define

    ell(A) = |A intersect B|,
    z(A) = 25*ell(A) + 24 (mod 101).

The inclusion matrix has one row for every (100)-element subset C
and one column for every (99)-element subset A.  Its (C,A) entry
is 1 when A is a subset of C and 0 otherwise.

Find a polynomial Q(x) over GF(101) of degree at most 99 such that,
for every (100)-element subset C of X, the exact identity

    sum over A subset C with |A|=p-2 of Q(z(A))

equals 69 when C is a subset of B, and equals 0 otherwise.
The sum is in GF(p).  The polynomial is unique under the degree bound.

Return Q as dense JSON polynomial data.  Include exactly one term
[coefficient,[exponent]] for every exponent 0,...,99, including zero
coefficients.  Term order is irrelevant; exponents may not repeat.
For example, 4+3x^2 is [[4,[0]],[0,[1]],[3,[2]]].

Give your final answer inside <answer></answer> tags, as that JSON list.
Example: <answer>[[4,[0]],[0,[1]],[3,[2]]]</answer>
Output nothing else inside the tags.
